questions.q: What do we call the motion of a pendulum where it moves to and fro about a fixed position?
questions.a: This is called oscillatory motion. A wrong answer like "linear motion" suggests the student does not recognize the "to and fro" nature of the swing, confusing it with simple straight-line travel.

questions.q: If you pull a pendulum bob a little further to the side than before, does the time taken for one full swing change significantly?
questions.a: No, the time (period) remains the same. A wrong answer suggests the student does not understand "isochronism," likely believing that a larger swing must inherently take more time, ignoring the property that period depends on length, not amplitude.

questions.q: A pendulum has a string of a certain length. If you replace the bob with a heavier one but keep the string length the same, what happens to the time for one swing?
questions.a: The time remains unchanged because the period is determined by the length of the string, not the weight of the bob. Answering that the time changes reveals a misconception that heavier objects must move slower or faster due to gravity's effect on mass.

questions.q: Why is a pendulum considered a good device for measuring time?
questions.a: It is useful because it is periodic, meaning it repeats its motion in equal intervals of time. If a student says "because it is heavy," they are failing to link the rhythm of the motion to the concept of time measurement.

questions.q: If two pendulums have different string lengths, will they have the same time period?
questions.a: No, the longer pendulum will take more time for a full swing. Answering "yes" shows the student has missed the key relationship that the period depends strictly on the length of the pendulum.

questions.q: Design a simple experiment to prove that a pendulum's period is independent of the push given to it (for small swings).
questions.a: The student should describe setting the pendulum in motion with a small pull, timing 10 swings with a stopwatch, then repeating the process with a slightly larger pull and comparing the average time per swing. A poor answer would suggest observing just one swing, which is too prone to human error to prove the consistency of the period.
